exam.label: Harmonic oscillator, ladder operators, coherent states

parts: The Hamiltonian of a particle in a one-dimensional harmonic potential is $H_0=\frac{p^2}{2m}+\frac12m\omega^2q^2$, $[q,p]=i\hbar$.
(i) Define $a=\sqrt{\frac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}\,q+\frac{i}{\sqrt{2m\hbar\omega}}\,p$. Show that $H_0=\hbar\omega(a^\dagger a+\frac12)$ and calculate $[a,a^\dagger]$. [3 pt]
(ii) Derive the energies $E_n$ and eigenstates $|n\rangle$ of this Hamiltonian using the ladder operators $a,a^\dagger$. [6 pt]
(iii) What property does the vacuum $|0\rangle$ satisfy? Use it to find the (normalised) wave function in position space. [4 pt]

items.title: Angular momentum spectrum from the algebra
items.goal: From $[\hat J_i,\hat J_j]=i\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}\hat J_k$ alone, show that $\hat{\mathbf J}^2$ has the eigenvalues $\hbar^2j(j+1)$ with $j\in\{0,\frac12,1,\dots\}$, and $\hat J_z$ the eigenvalues $\hbar m$, $m=-j,\dots,j$.
lines: $\hat J_\pm=\hat J_x\pm i\hat J_y$ obey $[\hat J_z,\hat J_\pm]=\pm\hbar\hat J_\pm$ and $[\hat{\mathbf J}^2,\hat J_\pm]=0$.
On common eigenstates $|\lambda,m\rangle$ ($\hat{\mathbf J}^2\to\hbar^2\lambda$, $\hat J_z\to\hbar m$), $\hat J_\pm$ changes $m$ by $\pm1$ and keeps $\lambda$.
$\hat J_\mp\hat J_\pm=\hat{\mathbf J}^2-\hat J_z^2\mp\hbar\hat J_z$, so $\|\hat J_\pm|\lambda,m\rangle\|^2=\hbar^2[\lambda-m(m\pm1)]\ge0$.
So $m$ is bounded. At the top $m=j$: $\hat J_+|\lambda,j\rangle=0$ gives $\lambda=j(j+1)$. At the bottom $m=j^\prime$: $\lambda=j^\prime(j^\prime-1)$, so $j^\prime=-j$.
From $-j$ to $j$ in integer steps: $2j\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}$, i.e. $j=0,\frac12,1,\frac32,\dots$, and $m=-j,-j+1,\dots,j$.
moves: Ladder operators shift $m$ by $\pm1$ and keep $\hat{\mathbf J}^2$
The squared norm of $\hat J_\pm|\lambda,m\rangle$ is $\hbar^2[\lambda-m(m\pm1)]\ge0$: $m$ is bounded
Top and bottom of the ladder give $\lambda=j(j+1)$ and $m_{\min}=-j$; integer steps give $2j\in\mathbb N_0$

whys.q: Why must the ladder stop at a top value $m=j$?
options: $\lambda-m(m+1)\ge0$ bounds $m$; if $\hat J_+|\lambda,j\rangle\ne0$ the next state would break the bound
The wave function must be single-valued
whys.explain: Single-valuedness is what later forbids half-integer $l$ for orbital angular momentum; the algebra alone allows half-integers.

whys.q: Where does the $\mp\hbar\hat J_z$ in $\hat J_\mp\hat J_\pm$ come from?
options: $\pm i[\hat J_x,\hat J_y]=\pm i\cdot i\hbar\hat J_z=\mp\hbar\hat J_z$
whys.explain: Multiply out $(\hat J_x\mp i\hat J_y)(\hat J_x\pm i\hat J_y)=\hat J_x^2+\hat J_y^2\pm i[\hat J_x,\hat J_y]$.

variant.change: Do not ask for the spectrum: ask for $\langle\hat L_x\rangle$ and $\langle\hat L_x^2\rangle$ in a state $|l,m\rangle$.
variant.changed: $\hat L_x=\frac12(\hat L_++\hat L_-)$ changes $m$, so its diagonal element vanishes; by symmetry $\langle\hat L_x^2\rangle=\langle\hat L_y^2\rangle=\frac12\langle\hat{\mathbf L}^2-\hat L_z^2\rangle$.

exam.label: Angular momentum algebra, rotations, spin-1/2 and spin-1

parts: The angular momentum operator is defined by $L_j=-i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}x_k\partial_{x_l}$, $j=1,2,3$.
(i) Show $[L_j,L_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}L_l$ (hint: work out $[L_1,L_2]$ and argue by symmetry). [2 pt]
(ii) With $L_\pm=L_1\pm iL_2$ compute $[L_3,L_\pm]$ and $[L_+,L_-]$ in terms of these generators. [2 pt]
(iii) In an irreducible representation $L_3|l,m\rangle=\hbar m|l,m\rangle$, $L_\pm|l,m\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{l(l+1)-m(m\pm1)}|l,m\pm1\rangle$. Show $\langle L_1\rangle=\langle L_2\rangle=0$. [3 pt]

Consider a single particle transforming in the representation $D_j$ of su(2). We choose an orthonormal basis of $D_j$ consisting of the vectors $|j,m\rangle$ that are eigenvectors of $S_z$ with eigenvalue $m$: $S_z|j,m\rangle=m|j,m\rangle$. Furthermore $S_\pm=S_x\pm iS_y$ acts as $S_\pm|j,m\rangle=\sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m\pm1)}\,|j,m\pm1\rangle$.
(i) Using $[S_x,S_y]=iS_z$, $[S_y,S_z]=iS_x$, $[S_z,S_x]=iS_y$, deduce the commutation relations $[S_z,S_\pm]$ and $[S_+,S_-]$. [2 points]
(ii) Using the formulas for $S_z$ and $S_\pm$ above, but not your result from (i), compute $[S_\pm,S_z]|j,m\rangle$ and $[S_+,S_-]|j,m\rangle$. Show that this agrees with (i). [3 points]

items.title: Coherent states of the oscillator
items.goal: Find the normalised eigenstates $|\alpha\rangle$ of $\hat a$, the distribution of $n$, and how $|\alpha\rangle$ evolves in time.
lines: Write $|\alpha\rangle=\sum_nc_n|n\rangle$. With $\hat a|n\rangle=\sqrt n|n-1\rangle$, $\hat a|\alpha\rangle=\alpha|\alpha\rangle$ gives $\sqrt{n+1}\,c_{n+1}=\alpha c_n$.
So $c_n=\frac{\alpha^n}{\sqrt{n!}}c_0$.
Normalise: $|c_0|^2\sum_n\frac{|\alpha|^{2n}}{n!}=|c_0|^2e^{|\alpha|^2}=1$, so $c_0=e^{-|\alpha|^2/2}$.
$P(n)=e^{-|\alpha|^2}\frac{|\alpha|^{2n}}{n!}$: a Poisson distribution with mean $\langle n\rangle=|\alpha|^2$.

In time, $c_n\to c_ne^{-i\omega(n+\frac12)t}$: this is $|\alpha e^{-i\omega t}\rangle$ times $e^{-i\omega t/2}$. It stays coherent, and $\langle\hat x\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{2\hbar}{m\omega}}\,\mathrm{Re}(\alpha e^{-i\omega t})$ oscillates classically.
moves: Expand in $|n\rangle$ and compare coefficients: a recursion
Normalise with the exponential series
Time evolution only rotates $\alpha$

whys.q: Why does $|\alpha\rangle$ remain an eigenstate of $\hat a$ in time?
options: Each $c_n$ picks up $(e^{-i\omega t})^n$ (apart from a common phase), which can be absorbed into $\alpha^n$
Because the Poisson distribution is stationary
whys.explain: $\hat a$ does not commute with $\hat H$ ($[\hat H,\hat a]=-\hbar\omega\hat a$), and $|\alpha\rangle$ is not stationary: the phases are equally spaced, which is what keeps the form.

variant.change: Look for eigenstates of $\hat a^\dagger$ instead of $\hat a$.
variant.changed: $\hat a^\dagger|\beta\rangle=\beta|\beta\rangle$ with $|\beta\rangle=\sum c_n|n\rangle$: the $|0\rangle$ component gives $\beta c_0=0$, and in general $\sqrt n\,c_{n-1}=\beta c_n$.
variant.result: For $\beta\ne0$: $c_0=0$, then $c_1=0$, and so on; for $\beta=0$: $c_{n-1}=0$ for all $n$. Only the zero vector: $\hat a^\dagger$ has no eigenstates.

items.title: Particle in an infinite well
items.goal: Infinite well on $0<x<a$: find the energies $E_n$ and the normalised $\psi_n$.
lines: Inside, $V=0$: $\psi^{\prime\prime}=-k^2\psi$ with $E=\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}$. Outside, $\psi=0$.
$\psi$ is continuous, so $\psi(0)=0$: $\psi=A\sin kx$.
$\psi(a)=0$: $ka=n\pi$ with $n=1,2,\dots$ ($n=0$ gives $\psi\equiv0$; negative $n$ repeat the same states).
$E_n=\frac{\hbar^2\pi^2n^2}{2ma^2}$, and $\int_0^a|A|^2\sin^2\frac{n\pi x}{a}dx=|A|^2\frac a2=1$ gives $\psi_n=\sqrt{\frac2a}\sin\frac{n\pi x}a$.
moves: Free particle inside, zero outside
The wall at 0 picks $\sin kx$
The wall at $a$ quantises $k$
Normalise

whys.q: Why must $\psi(0)=0$, although $\psi^\prime$ may jump there?
options: $\psi$ must be continuous; $\psi^\prime$ may jump because the potential jumps by an infinite amount
whys.explain: A jump in $\psi$ would make $\psi^\prime$ a delta function and the kinetic energy infinite. At an infinite wall only $\psi$ is matched, not $\psi^\prime$.

whys.q: Why is $n=0$ not a state?
options: The uncertainty principle forbids zero energy
whys.explain: The uncertainty argument explains why the ground state energy is positive, but the formal reason is simply that $\sin0=0$ everywhere.

variant.change: Same width, but the well sits at $-\frac a2<x<\frac a2$.
variant.changed: Use parity: even solutions $\cos kx$ need $\cos\frac{ka}2=0$, odd ones $\sin kx$ need $\sin\frac{ka}2=0$.
variant.result: The energies are the same, $E_n=\frac{\hbar^2\pi^2n^2}{2ma^2}$. $\psi_n=\sqrt{\frac2a}\cos\frac{n\pi x}a$ for odd $n$ and $\sqrt{\frac2a}\sin\frac{n\pi x}a$ for even $n$: the old states, shifted by $a/2$.

exam.label: 1D box, finite well, parity, bound-state existence

parts: Consider a particle in 1d, confined to a box of length $a$. The Hamiltonian is $H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2+V(x)$ with $V=0$ for $x\in[0,a]$ and $V=\infty$ else.

(i) Find the (normalised) eigenfunctions $\psi_n$ and the associated eigenvalues $E_n$ of the Hamiltonian for the particle in the box. What boundary conditions does the wave function have to satisfy? [5 points]

We consider a particle of mass $m$ moving in a 2-dimensional box of size $a$ with coordinates $0\le x\le a$ and $0\le y\le a$. The potential vanishes inside the box, and the wave function vanishes at the edges.
(i) Find the normalised eigenfunctions of the Hamilton operator and the associated energies. [6 pt]

items.title: Finite well: even states always exist
items.goal: $V=-V_0$ for $|x|<\frac a2$, zero outside. Derive the condition for the even bound states and show that at least one always exists.
lines: Inside: $\psi^{\prime\prime}=-k^2\psi$ with $k=\frac{\sqrt{2m(E+V_0)}}\hbar$; outside: $\psi\propto e^{-\kappa|x|}$ with $\kappa=\frac{\sqrt{-2mE}}\hbar$.
$V$ is even, so the bound states are even or odd; even: $\psi=\cos kx$ inside.
Match $\psi^\prime/\psi$ at $x=\frac a2$: $-k\tan\frac{ka}2=-\kappa$.
With $z=\frac{ka}2$ and $z_0=\frac a2\frac{\sqrt{2mV_0}}\hbar$ ($k^2+\kappa^2=\frac{2mV_0}{\hbar^2}$): $\tan z=\sqrt{\frac{z_0^2}{z^2}-1}$.
The left side rises from 0, the right side falls from $+\infty$ to 0 at $z=z_0$: they always cross once in $0<z<\min(z_0,\frac\pi2)$. At least one even bound state for any depth.
moves: Solve inside and outside
Use parity: even states first
Match the logarithmic derivative
Dimensionless graphical solution: always one crossing

whys.q: Why may we look for even and odd solutions separately?
options: Parity commutes with $\hat H$ when $V(-x)=V(x)$, and 1D bound states are non-degenerate, so each is even or odd
Because cosines and sines are a basis
whys.explain: In general only eigenstates can be chosen with definite parity; in 1D bound states are non-degenerate, so they automatically have it.

whys.q: Why match $\psi^\prime/\psi$ instead of $\psi$ and $\psi^\prime$ separately?
options: It removes the unknown amplitudes in one equation
It is only valid for even states
whys.explain: Both $\psi$ and $\psi^\prime$ are continuous at a finite step; their ratio is too, and it does not depend on the normalisation of either side.

variant.change: Ask for the first odd bound state instead.
variant.changed: Odd: $\sin kx$ inside, and the matching gives $\cot z=-\frac{\sqrt{z_0^2-z^2}}z$, which needs $\cot z<0$, i.e. $z>\frac\pi2$.
variant.result: Only if $z_0>\frac\pi2$, i.e. $V_0a^2>\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}$: a minimum depth. (The same condition decides whether a 3D square well binds an $s$-wave, since there $u(0)=0$ as for odd states.)

exam.label: 1D box, finite well, parity, bound-state existence

parts: A point particle of mass $m$ in the symmetric well $V(x)=-V_0$ for $-a<x<a$, $0$ otherwise ($0<V_0<\infty$). Bound states have $E<0$ and can be written $\psi=Ae^{\eta x/a}$ ($x<-a$), $B\sin\frac{\xi}ax+C\cos\frac{\xi}ax$ ($|x|\le a$), $De^{-\eta x/a}$ ($x>a$), with $\xi,\eta>0$.
(a) Express $\eta$ and $\xi$ through $E$, $V_0$ and $a$. [3]
(b) Show that $\xi^2+\eta^2=\frac{2mV_0a^2}{\hbar^2}$. [2] (Continuity then gives $\eta=-\xi\frac{B\cos\xi-C\sin\xi}{B\sin\xi+C\cos\xi}$, which may be used.)
(c) Show from the Schrödinger equation that $\psi$ is necessarily even or odd (use $V(-x)=V(x)$ and that bound states are non-degenerate). [8]
(d) Show graphically that at least one bound state always exists. [8]
(e) Find the condition on $V_0$ for exactly one bound state. Which parity does it have? [4]

items.title: Non-degenerate perturbation theory to second order
items.goal: $\hat H=\hat H_0+\lambda\hat V$ with non-degenerate $\hat H_0|n\rangle=E_n^{(0)}|n\rangle$. Derive $E_n^{(1)}$, $|n^{(1)}\rangle$ and $E_n^{(2)}$.
lines: Expand $|n(\lambda)\rangle=|n\rangle+\lambda|n^{(1)}\rangle+\dots$ and $E_n=E_n^{(0)}+\lambda E_n^{(1)}+\lambda^2E_n^{(2)}+\dots$, with the choice $\langle n|n^{(1)}\rangle=0$.
Order $\lambda$: $(\hat H_0-E_n^{(0)})|n^{(1)}\rangle=(E_n^{(1)}-\hat V)|n\rangle$.
Project on $\langle n|$: the left side vanishes, so $E_n^{(1)}=\langle n|\hat V|n\rangle$.
Project on $\langle m|$, $m\ne n$: $\langle m|n^{(1)}\rangle=\frac{\langle m|\hat V|n\rangle}{E_n^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)}}$.
Order $\lambda^2$, projected on $\langle n|$: $E_n^{(2)}=\langle n|\hat V|n^{(1)}\rangle=\sum_{m\ne n}\frac{|\langle m|\hat V|n\rangle|^2}{E_n^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)}}$.
moves: Expand in $\lambda$ and sort by order
Project on $\langle n|$: the $\hat H_0$ term drops, first-order energy
Project on $\langle m|$: the state correction
Second order is $\langle n|\hat V|n^{(1)}\rangle$

whys.q: Why does the left side vanish when you project on $\langle n|$?
options: $\langle n|(\hat H_0-E_n^{(0)})=0$, because $\hat H_0$ is Hermitian and acts to the left
whys.explain: The gauge choice $\langle n|n^{(1)}\rangle=0$ is not needed for this step; Hermiticity alone kills it.

whys.q: Why is the second-order shift of the ground state never positive?
options: Every numerator $|\langle m|\hat V|0\rangle|^2$ is $\ge0$ and every denominator $E_0^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)}$ is negative
By the variational principle applied to first order
whys.explain: Only for the ground state are all denominators negative; excited levels can be pushed either way (level repulsion).

variant.change: The level $E_n^{(0)}$ is twofold degenerate, with states $|n,1\rangle$ and $|n,2\rangle$.
variant.task: What goes wrong, and what replaces $E_n^{(1)}=\langle n|\hat V|n\rangle$?
variant.changed: The state correction divides by $E_n^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)}=0$ for the partner state, unless $\langle n,a|\hat V|n,b\rangle=0$ for $a\ne b$.
variant.result: Choose the zeroth-order states as the eigenvectors of the $2\times2$ matrix $V_{ab}=\langle n,a|\hat V|n,b\rangle$; the first-order shifts are its eigenvalues, $\det(V_{ab}-E^{(1)}\delta_{ab})=0$.

parts: In this question we study time-independent non-degenerate perturbation theory.

(i) Let $H_0$ be a Hamiltonian whose complete set of eigenfunctions is described by $H_0\psi_n=E_n\psi_n$, $n=0,1,2,\dots$, where $E_n\neq E_m$ for $n\ne m$. We want to find the eigenfunctions of the perturbed Hamiltonian $H=H_0+\lambda H'$. Make an ansatz for $\psi$ and $E$ as a power series in $\lambda$ and determine the equations order by order in $\lambda$ (up to $\lambda^2$). Explain how to find the perturbed eigenfunction $\psi$ to first order in $\lambda$ and the corresponding eigenvalue to second order in $\lambda$. (You should work with the convention that the higher order corrections to the eigenfunction are orthogonal to the leading term.) [10 pt]

Let $H_0$ be a Hamiltonian whose complete set of eigenfunctions is described by $H_0\psi_n=E_n\psi_n$, $n=0,1,2,\dots$. We want to find the eigenfunctions of the perturbed Hamiltonian $H=H_0+\lambda H'$.

(i) Let $\psi$ be an eigenstate of the perturbed system with energy $E$. Make an ansatz for $\psi$ and $E$ as a power series in $\lambda$, and derive the equations for the perturbation at any order $\lambda^s$. [5 pt] [Hint: Derive a general equation that holds for $s\ge2$, and then treat the cases $s=0$ and $s=1$ separately.]

items.title: Two spins: eigenvalues of $\hat{\mathbf S}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_2$, triplet and singlet
items.goal: Two spins $\frac12$: find the eigenvalues of $\hat{\mathbf S}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_2$ and the eigenstates.
lines: $\hat{\mathbf S}^2=(\hat{\mathbf S}_1+\hat{\mathbf S}_2)^2=\hat{\mathbf S}_1^2+\hat{\mathbf S}_2^2+2\hat{\mathbf S}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_2$.
$\hat{\mathbf S}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_2=\frac12(\hat{\mathbf S}^2-\hat{\mathbf S}_1^2-\hat{\mathbf S}_2^2)=\frac{\hbar^2}2\big[S(S+1)-\frac32\big]$ on states of total spin $S$.
$\frac12\otimes\frac12$: $S=1$ (three states) or $S=0$ (one state); count: $2\cdot2=3+1$.

Triplet: $|1,1\rangle=|\!\uparrow\uparrow\rangle$; lowering with $\hat S_-=\hat S_{1-}+\hat S_{2-}$ gives $|1,0\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt2}(|\!\uparrow\downarrow\rangle+|\!\downarrow\uparrow\rangle)$ and $|1,-1\rangle=|\!\downarrow\downarrow\rangle$. Eigenvalue $+\frac{\hbar^2}4$.
Singlet: the $m=0$ state orthogonal to $|1,0\rangle$, $\frac1{\sqrt2}(|\!\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-|\!\downarrow\uparrow\rangle)$. Eigenvalue $-\frac{3\hbar^2}4$.
moves: Complete the square: $\hat{\mathbf S}^2$
Eigenvalues from $S(S+1)$
Top state, lower it, then the orthogonal partner

whys.q: Why is $(\hat{\mathbf S}_1+\hat{\mathbf S}_2)^2=\hat{\mathbf S}_1^2+\hat{\mathbf S}_2^2+2\hat{\mathbf S}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_2$, without worrying about the order?
whys.explain: The cross terms are $\hat{\mathbf S}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_2+\hat{\mathbf S}_2\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_1$, and these are equal because each component of spin 1 commutes with each component of spin 2.

whys.q: Why is the singlet the antisymmetric combination?
options: It must be orthogonal to $|1,0\rangle$ and have $m=0$; only one such state exists
whys.explain: Fermion antisymmetry concerns the full state including space; here it is just orthogonality inside the $m=0$ subspace.

variant.change: Spin $\frac12$ with orbital angular momentum $l=1$: $\hat{\mathbf L}\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}$ (fine structure).
variant.task: Find the eigenvalues of $\hat{\mathbf L}\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}$ and the multiplets.
variant.changed: $\hat{\mathbf J}=\hat{\mathbf L}+\hat{\mathbf S}$ and $\hat{\mathbf L}\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}=\frac12(\hat{\mathbf J}^2-\hat{\mathbf L}^2-\hat{\mathbf S}^2)$, with $j=\frac32$ or $\frac12$.

items.title: Virial theorem from a commutator
items.goal: In a stationary state of $\hat H=\frac{\hat p^2}{2m}+V(\hat x)$, show $2\langle\hat T\rangle=\langle\hat xV^\prime(\hat x)\rangle$.
lines: In an eigenstate of $\hat H$, $\langle[\hat H,\hat A]\rangle=0$ for every $\hat A$. Take $\hat A=\hat x\hat p$.
$\big[\frac{\hat p^2}{2m},\hat x\hat p\big]=\frac1{2m}[\hat p^2,\hat x]\hat p=-\frac{i\hbar}m\hat p^2$.
$[V(\hat x),\hat x\hat p]=\hat x[V,\hat p]=i\hbar\,\hat xV^\prime(\hat x)$.
$0=\langle[\hat H,\hat x\hat p]\rangle=-\frac{i\hbar}m\langle\hat p^2\rangle+i\hbar\langle\hat xV^\prime\rangle$, so $2\langle\hat T\rangle=\langle\hat xV^\prime\rangle$.
For $V\propto|x|^s$: $xV^\prime=sV$, so $2\langle T\rangle=s\langle V\rangle$. Oscillator ($s=2$): $\langle T\rangle=\langle V\rangle=\frac E2$.
moves: Stationary state: $\langle[\hat H,\hat A]\rangle=0$
Choose $\hat A=\hat x\hat p$
Two commutators: $-\frac{i\hbar}m\hat p^2$ and $i\hbar\,\hat xV^\prime$

whys.q: Why is $\langle[\hat H,\hat A]\rangle=0$ in an eigenstate of $\hat H$?
options: $\langle E|\hat H\hat A-\hat A\hat H|E\rangle=E\langle\hat A\rangle-E\langle\hat A\rangle=0$
Because $\hat x\hat p$ commutes with $\hat H$
whys.explain: $\hat x\hat p$ is not even Hermitian, and the argument does not need it: $\hat H$ acts on the eigenstate to the left and to the right.

whys.q: Why is $[V(\hat x),\hat p]=i\hbar V^\prime(\hat x)$?
options: On a test function: $V(-i\hbar f^\prime)+i\hbar(Vf)^\prime=i\hbar V^\prime f$
Because $[\hat x,\hat p]=i\hbar$ and $V$ is linear
whys.explain: It holds for any differentiable $V$; the product rule does the work.

variant.change: Three dimensions, hydrogen: $V=-\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}$ and $\hat A=\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf p}$.
variant.result: $2\langle T\rangle=-\langle V\rangle$, so $E=\langle T\rangle+\langle V\rangle=-\langle T\rangle=\frac12\langle V\rangle$. For the ground state: $\langle T\rangle=13.6$ eV, $\langle V\rangle=-27.2$ eV.

asked.exam: exam style (no old exam or sheet asks it verbatim)
parts: $H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+V(x)$ and a normalised stationary state $\psi$, $H\psi=E\psi$.
(i) Show that $\langle\psi|[H,A]|\psi\rangle=0$ for every operator $A$. [2]
(ii) Use $A=xp$ to derive the virial theorem $2\langle T\rangle=\langle xV^\prime(x)\rangle$. [4]
(iii) Apply it to the harmonic oscillator and to $V\propto|x|^n$: how are $\langle T\rangle$, $\langle V\rangle$ and $E$ related? [2]

where.note: Not in the script. It uses the same idea as Ehrenfest (2.3): the time derivative of an expectation value vanishes in a stationary state.

items.title: Heisenberg picture: the oscillator operators in time
items.goal: Show $\frac{d}{dt}\hat A_H=\frac i\hbar[\hat H,\hat A_H]$ and solve it for $\hat x_H(t)$, $\hat p_H(t)$ and $\hat a_H(t)$ of the harmonic oscillator.
lines: $\hat U=e^{-i\hat Ht/\hbar}$, $\hat A_H(t)=\hat U^\dagger\hat A\hat U$; since $\hat H$ commutes with $\hat U$: $\frac{d}{dt}\hat A_H=\frac i\hbar\hat U^\dagger[\hat H,\hat A]\hat U=\frac i\hbar[\hat H,\hat A_H]$.
$[\hat H,\hat x]=-\frac{i\hbar}m\hat p$ and $[\hat H,\hat p]=\big[\frac12m\omega^2\hat x^2,\hat p\big]=i\hbar m\omega^2\hat x$.
So $\dot{\hat x}_H=\frac{\hat p_H}m$ and $\dot{\hat p}_H=-m\omega^2\hat x_H$: the classical equations, now for operators.
$\hat x_H(t)=\hat x\cos\omega t+\frac{\hat p}{m\omega}\sin\omega t$, $\hat p_H(t)=\hat p\cos\omega t-m\omega\hat x\sin\omega t$.
$[\hat H,\hat a]=-\hbar\omega\hat a$, so $\dot{\hat a}_H=-i\omega\hat a_H$ and $\hat a_H(t)=\hat a\,e^{-i\omega t}$.
moves: Differentiate $\hat U^\dagger\hat A\hat U$: the commutator with $\hat H$
Two commutators give operator versions of Newton
Solve like the classical oscillator, with the initial operators as constants

whys.q: Why are expectation values the same in both pictures?
options: $\langle\psi(t)|\hat A|\psi(t)\rangle=\langle\psi(0)|\hat U^\dagger\hat A\hat U|\psi(0)\rangle$: the time dependence is only moved from the state to the operator
Because the states do not change
whys.explain: $\hat U$ is unitary, not Hermitian; that is why it can be moved from the ket and bra onto the operator.

variant.change: Replace the oscillator by a constant force: $\hat H=\frac{\hat p^2}{2m}-F\hat x$.
variant.changed: $[\hat H,\hat p]=-F[\hat x,\hat p]=-i\hbar F$, so $\dot{\hat p}_H=F$, and still $\dot{\hat x}_H=\hat p_H/m$.
variant.result: $\hat p_H(t)=\hat p+Ft$ and $\hat x_H(t)=\hat x+\frac{\hat p}mt+\frac{F}{2m}t^2$: the wave packet’s centre falls like a classical particle, and its width grows as for a free particle.

parts: Let $\hat H=\frac{\hat P^2}{2m}+\frac12m\omega^2\hat X^2$ be the Hamiltonian of the 1D harmonic oscillator and $|n\rangle$ the Fock states.

(c) Show that in the Heisenberg picture $\hat X_H(t)=\hat X\cos\omega t+\frac{\hat P}{m\omega}\sin\omega t$ and $\hat P_H(t)=-m\omega\hat X\sin\omega t+\hat P\cos\omega t$. Hint: find expressions for $d\hat X_H/dt$, $d\hat P_H/dt$ and solve the coupled differential equations. [8 pt]

(i) State the time-dependent Schrodinger equation, and write down the solution with initial state $\Psi(t_0)$ as $\Psi(t)=U(t,t_0)\Psi(t_0)$. Deduce the differential equation the propagator $U(t,t_0)$ has to solve, and construct its (formal) solution. [5 pt]
(ii) Explain how to define the Heisenberg picture, and deduce the equations of motion of an operator in the Heisenberg picture. [3 pt]
(iii) Determine the condition for an observable $A$ that does not depend explicitly on time, to be conserved. [2 pt]

items.title: Clebsch–Gordan coefficients for $1\otimes\frac12$
items.goal: Couple $l=1$ and $s=\frac12$: find the states $|j,m\rangle$ with $m=\frac12$ in terms of $|m_l\rangle|m_s\rangle$.
lines: $j=\frac32$ (4 states) or $j=\frac12$ (2 states): $3\cdot2=4+2$.
The only product state with $m=\frac32$ is $|1\rangle|\!\uparrow\rangle$, so $|\tfrac32,\tfrac32\rangle=|1\rangle|\!\uparrow\rangle$.

$\hat J_-|\tfrac32,\tfrac32\rangle=\hbar\sqrt3\,|\tfrac32,\tfrac12\rangle$ and $(\hat L_-+\hat S_-)|1\rangle|\!\uparrow\rangle=\hbar\sqrt2\,|0\rangle|\!\uparrow\rangle+\hbar\,|1\rangle|\!\downarrow\rangle$.
So $|\tfrac32,\tfrac12\rangle=\sqrt{\tfrac23}\,|0\rangle|\!\uparrow\rangle+\sqrt{\tfrac13}\,|1\rangle|\!\downarrow\rangle$.

$|\tfrac12,\tfrac12\rangle$ is the orthogonal $m=\frac12$ combination: $\sqrt{\tfrac23}\,|1\rangle|\!\downarrow\rangle-\sqrt{\tfrac13}\,|0\rangle|\!\uparrow\rangle$ (overall sign by the Condon–Shortley convention).
moves: Count the multiplets
Start at the top: the unique product state
Lower with $\hat J_-=\hat L_-+\hat S_-$ and compare both sides
The orthogonal partner starts the next multiplet

whys.q: Where do $\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt2$ come from?
options: $\hbar\sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m-1)}$ for $\hat J_-$ on $|\tfrac32,\tfrac32\rangle$ and for $\hat L_-$ on $|1,1\rangle$
whys.explain: $\frac{15}4-\frac34=3$ and $2-0=2$; for $\hat S_-|\!\uparrow\rangle$ the root is $\sqrt{\frac34+\frac14}=1$.

variant.changed: $j=2,1,0$ ($9=5+3+1$); top $|2,2\rangle=|1\rangle|1\rangle$; $\hat J_-$ gives $2\hbar|2,1\rangle$ on the left and $\sqrt2\hbar(|0\rangle|1\rangle+|1\rangle|0\rangle)$ on the right.

parts: Question 3 [Clebsch-Gordan coefficients] (i) Prove that the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients for the decomposition of the tensor product of spin $l$ and spin $\frac12$ to spin $l+\frac12$ are $\langle l,\tfrac12,m\mp\tfrac12,\pm\tfrac12|l,\tfrac12,l+\tfrac12,m\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{l\pm m+\frac12}{2l+1}}$. Hint: First focus on the $m_2=\frac12$ coefficients. Using one of the recursion relations from the lecture show that $\langle l,\tfrac12,m-\tfrac32,\tfrac12|l,\tfrac12,l+\tfrac12,m-1\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{l+m-\frac12}{l+m+\frac12}}\langle l,\tfrac12,m-\tfrac12,\tfrac12|l,\tfrac12,l+\tfrac12,m\rangle$. Identify the state of highest spin, then use this relation to find all the $m_2=\frac12$ coefficients. To find the $m_2=-\frac12$ coefficients, consider the other recursion relation from the lecture.

(ii) An electron in the hydrogen atom is in an orbital angular momentum state with $l=1$. Find the eigenstates of the total (orbital and spin) angular momentum $|j,j_z\rangle$ in $D_{3/2}$ in terms of those labelled by $|m,s\rangle$, where $m$ and $s$ are the $z$-components of the orbital and spin angular momentum operators, respectively.

items.title: Bound state of the delta well
lines: For $x\ne0$: $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi^{\prime\prime}=E\psi$ with $E<0$, so $\psi\propto e^{\pm\kappa x}$ with $\kappa=\frac{\sqrt{-2mE}}\hbar$.
Normalisable and continuous at 0: $\psi=A\,e^{-\kappa|x|}$.
Integrate the Schrödinger equation from $-\epsilon$ to $\epsilon$: $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\big[\psi^\prime(0^+)-\psi^\prime(0^-)\big]-\alpha\psi(0)=0$.
With $\psi^\prime(0^+)-\psi^\prime(0^-)=-2\kappa A$ and $\psi(0)=A$: $\kappa=\frac{m\alpha}{\hbar^2}$.
$E=-\frac{\hbar^2\kappa^2}{2m}=-\frac{m\alpha^2}{2\hbar^2}$ and $A=\sqrt\kappa$.
moves: Solve outside the delta: decaying exponentials
Normalisable and continuous: $e^{-\kappa|x|}$
Integrate across the delta: the kink in $\psi^\prime$ fixes $\kappa$

whys.q: Why may the $E\psi$ term be dropped when integrating from $-\epsilon$ to $\epsilon$?
options: $\psi$ is bounded, so $\int_{-\epsilon}^{\epsilon}E\psi\,dx\to0$; only the delta survives
whys.explain: $\psi^\prime$ is exactly what is not continuous here: its jump is the whole point of the step.

variant.result: $e^{-\kappa|x|}$ with $\kappa<0$ grows at infinity: not normalisable, so there is no bound state.

parts: A particle in the one-dimensional potential $V(x)=V_1\Theta(x)-V_0\delta(x)$ with $V_{0,1}>0$ ($\Theta$ the Heaviside step).
a) The potential has at most one bound state. Find it and its energy, and show that it exists only if $\frac{2mV_0}{\hbar^2}>\frac{V_1}{V_0}$. [4 P]
b) Compute the energy correction of the bound state of the pure $\delta$ potential to the first non-vanishing order, treating the step as a perturbation with $V_1\ll V_0$. [1 P]

where.note: The delta potential itself is not in the script; it is sheet 4 Q1 (with the official solution). The matching method is the one of 3.2-3.3.

items.title: Central potential: separation and the radial equation
items.goal: For $\hat H=\frac{\hat{\mathbf p}^2}{2m}+V(r)$, separate the variables and derive the radial equation for $u(r)=rR(r)$.
lines: $\hat{\mathbf p}^2=-\hbar^2\nabla^2=-\hbar^2\frac1r\partial_r^2\,r+\frac{\hat{\mathbf L}^2}{r^2}$.
$\hat{\mathbf L}^2$ and $\hat L_z$ act only on the angles and commute with $\hat H$: $\psi=R(r)\,Y_{lm}(\theta,\varphi)$ with $\hat{\mathbf L}^2\to\hbar^2l(l+1)$.
With $u=rR$: $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}u^{\prime\prime}+\Big[V(r)+\frac{\hbar^2l(l+1)}{2mr^2}\Big]u=Eu$.
Boundary conditions: $u(0)=0$ (so that $R$ stays finite) and $\int_0^\infty|u|^2dr=1$.
The energy does not depend on $m$: every level is at least $(2l+1)$-fold degenerate.
moves: Split $\nabla^2$ into a radial part and $\hat{\mathbf L}^2/r^2$
Angular part: $Y_{lm}$
$u=rR$ turns it into a 1D problem with the centrifugal term

whys.q: Why can $E$ not depend on $m$?
options: $\hat L_\pm$ commute with $\hat H$ and change only $m$, so all $2l+1$ states of a multiplet have the same energy
Because $V$ depends only on $r$ and $m$ does not appear in $V$
whys.explain: Conservation of $\hat L_z$ alone would allow $E$ to depend on $m$; it is the full rotation symmetry (all $\hat L_i$, hence $\hat L_\pm$) that forces the degeneracy.

variant.change: An infinite spherical well ($V=0$ for $r<a$, infinite outside), and only $l=0$.
variant.changed: For $l=0$ there is no centrifugal term: $u^{\prime\prime}=-k^2u$ with $u(0)=0$ and $u(a)=0$.
variant.result: $u=\sin kr$, $ka=n\pi$: $E_n=\frac{\hbar^2\pi^2n^2}{2ma^2}$, the same numbers as the 1D box, with $R=\frac{\sin kr}{r}$ finite at the centre.

exam.label: 3D wave mechanics, central potentials, radial equation

asked.exam: HS16 (3D oscillator in spherical coordinates, translated)
parts: $H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Delta+\frac{m\omega^2}2r^2$.
(b) Write $H$ in spherical coordinates. With $\Psi(r,\theta,\varphi)=R(r)Y_{lm}(\theta,\varphi)$ derive the differential equation for $R(r)$. What motivates this separation ansatz? [1.5 P]

With $R=u/r$: $\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dr^2}+V_{\rm eff}\right)u=Eu$, $V_{\rm eff}=\frac{\hbar^2l(l+1)}{2mr^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}2r^2$; $u(0)=0$ may be used. (c) Sketch $V_{\rm eff}$: what about bound and unbound states? [0.5 P]
(d) The equation for $r\to0$ and its solution (ansatz $u\sim r^\alpha$). [1 P] (e) The equation for $r\to\infty$: which known problem is it, and how does $u$ behave? [1.5 P]

items.title: General uncertainty relation
items.goal: For Hermitian $\hat A,\hat B$ and a normalised state, show $\Delta A\,\Delta B\ge\frac12\big|\langle[\hat A,\hat B]\rangle\big|$.
lines: Shift to zero mean: $\hat a=\hat A-\langle A\rangle$, $\hat b=\hat B-\langle B\rangle$. Then $\Delta A^2=\langle\hat a^2\rangle=\|\hat a\psi\|^2$ and $[\hat a,\hat b]=[\hat A,\hat B]$.
Cauchy–Schwarz: $\|\hat a\psi\|^2\,\|\hat b\psi\|^2\ge|\langle\hat a\psi|\hat b\psi\rangle|^2=|\langle\hat a\hat b\rangle|^2$.
$|z|^2\ge(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^2$, and $\mathrm{Im}\langle\hat a\hat b\rangle=\frac1{2i}\langle\hat a\hat b-\hat b\hat a\rangle$ because $\langle\hat b\hat a\rangle=\langle\hat a\hat b\rangle^*$.
So $\Delta A^2\,\Delta B^2\ge\frac14|\langle[\hat A,\hat B]\rangle|^2$; take the square root.
moves: Shift to zero mean (the commutator does not change)
Cauchy–Schwarz on $\hat a\psi$ and $\hat b\psi$
Keep only the imaginary part: it is the commutator

whys.q: Why is $\langle\hat a\psi|\hat b\psi\rangle=\langle\hat a\hat b\rangle$?
options: $\hat a$ is Hermitian, so it moves to the other side unchanged
whys.explain: $\langle\hat a\psi|\hat b\psi\rangle=\langle\psi|\hat a^\dagger\hat b\psi\rangle$ with $\hat a^\dagger=\hat a$. They do not commute in general: that is the point.

whys.q: Why may the real part be dropped?
options: The real part vanishes for Hermitian operators
The real part is the anticommutator, which is zero
Because the result must be real
whys.explain: The real part is $\frac12\langle\{\hat a,\hat b\}\rangle$, a covariance, and it is not zero in general. Dropping it only weakens the bound (keeping it gives the Schrödinger–Robertson relation).

variant.change: Take $\hat A=\hat L_x$, $\hat B=\hat L_y$ in a state $|l,m\rangle$.
variant.task: What does the bound say, and when is it saturated?
variant.changed: $[\hat L_x,\hat L_y]=i\hbar\hat L_z$, and in $|l,m\rangle$: $\Delta L_x^2=\Delta L_y^2=\frac{\hbar^2}2[l(l+1)-m^2]$.
variant.result: The bound is $\Delta L_x\Delta L_y\ge\frac{\hbar^2}2|m|$. The product is $\frac{\hbar^2}2[l(l+1)-m^2]$, and $l(l+1)-m^2-|m|=(l-|m|)(l+|m|+1)\ge0$: equality exactly for $|m|=l$.

parts: Suppose $A$ and $B$ are two self-adjoint operators acting on a Hilbert space. We define the variance of $A$ via $(\Delta A)_\psi\equiv\sqrt{\langle(A-\langle A\rangle_\psi)^2\rangle_\psi}$, where the expectation value is taken with respect to some state $\psi$ in the Hilbert space.
(i) Prove that $i[A,B]$ and $\{A,B\}\equiv AB+BA$ are hermitian operators. [2 pt]
(ii) Prove the Heisenberg uncertainty relation $(\Delta A)_\psi(\Delta B)_\psi\ge\frac12|\langle i[A,B]\rangle_\psi|$. [4 pt]

items.title: Ehrenfest theorem
items.goal: Show $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\hat x\rangle=\frac{\langle\hat p\rangle}m$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\hat p\rangle=-\langle V^\prime(\hat x)\rangle$ for $\hat H=\frac{\hat p^2}{2m}+V(\hat x)$.
lines: From $i\hbar\,\partial_t|\psi\rangle=\hat H|\psi\rangle$: $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\hat A\rangle=\frac i\hbar\langle[\hat H,\hat A]\rangle$ for $\hat A$ without explicit time dependence.
$[\hat H,\hat x]=\frac1{2m}[\hat p^2,\hat x]=\frac1{2m}\big(\hat p[\hat p,\hat x]+[\hat p,\hat x]\hat p\big)=-\frac{i\hbar}m\hat p$.
$\frac{d}{dt}\langle\hat x\rangle=\frac i\hbar\cdot\big(-\frac{i\hbar}m\big)\langle\hat p\rangle=\frac{\langle\hat p\rangle}m$.
$[\hat H,\hat p]=[V(\hat x),\hat p]=i\hbar V^\prime(\hat x)$ (act on a test function).
$\frac{d}{dt}\langle\hat p\rangle=\frac i\hbar\cdot i\hbar\langle V^\prime\rangle=-\langle V^\prime(\hat x)\rangle$.
moves: $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\hat A\rangle=\frac i\hbar\langle[\hat H,\hat A]\rangle$
$[\hat p^2,\hat x]=-2i\hbar\hat p$
$[V(\hat x),\hat p]=i\hbar V^\prime$ on a test function

whys.q: Where does $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\hat A\rangle=\frac i\hbar\langle[\hat H,\hat A]\rangle$ come from?
options: Product rule on $\langle\psi|\hat A|\psi\rangle$ with $\partial_t|\psi\rangle=-\frac i\hbar\hat H|\psi\rangle$ and $\partial_t\langle\psi|=\frac i\hbar\langle\psi|\hat H$
whys.explain: The bra picks up $+\frac i\hbar\hat H$ because $\hat H$ is Hermitian; the two terms combine to the commutator.

variant.task: When do $\langle x\rangle$ and $\langle p\rangle$ obey Newton’s equations exactly?
variant.changed: Everything hinges on $\langle V^\prime(\hat x)\rangle$ versus $V^\prime(\langle\hat x\rangle)$.
variant.result: Oscillator: $\langle V^\prime\rangle=m\omega^2\langle x\rangle=V^\prime(\langle x\rangle)$, exactly classical. Quartic: $\langle V^\prime\rangle=4\lambda\langle x^3\rangle\ne4\lambda\langle x\rangle^3$ in general. Exactly classical only when $V^\prime$ is at most linear.

parts: Consider a particle of mass $m$ moving in one dimension subject to a potential $V(x)$.
(i) State the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, and deduce Ehrenfest's theorem $\frac d{dt}\langle x\rangle=\frac1m\langle p\rangle$. [5 pt]

items.title: Probability current and the continuity equation
items.goal: Show $\partial_t|\psi|^2+\partial_xj=0$ with $j=\frac\hbar m\mathrm{Im}(\psi^*\partial_x\psi)$, for a real potential $V$.
lines: $\partial_t\rho=\psi^*\partial_t\psi+\psi\,\partial_t\psi^*$ with $\rho=|\psi|^2$.
$\partial_t\psi=\frac{i\hbar}{2m}\psi^{\prime\prime}-\frac i\hbar V\psi$ and $\partial_t\psi^*=-\frac{i\hbar}{2m}\psi^{*\prime\prime}+\frac i\hbar V\psi^*$.
The potential terms cancel: $-\frac i\hbar V|\psi|^2+\frac i\hbar V|\psi|^2=0$.
$\partial_t\rho=\frac{i\hbar}{2m}\big(\psi^*\psi^{\prime\prime}-\psi\psi^{*\prime\prime}\big)=\frac{i\hbar}{2m}\partial_x\big(\psi^*\psi^\prime-\psi\psi^{*\prime}\big)$.
$\psi^*\psi^\prime-\psi\psi^{*\prime}=2i\,\mathrm{Im}(\psi^*\psi^\prime)$, so $\partial_t\rho=-\partial_x\big[\frac\hbar m\mathrm{Im}(\psi^*\psi^\prime)\big]$.
moves: Product rule on $\psi^*\psi$
Insert the Schrödinger equation and its conjugate: $V$ cancels
Write the rest as a total derivative

whys.q: Why do the potential terms cancel?
options: $V$ is real, so the two terms are $\mp\frac i\hbar V|\psi|^2$
whys.explain: With a complex $V$ they do not cancel: that is how absorption is modelled (see the variant).

whys.q: Why is $\psi^*\psi^{\prime\prime}-\psi\psi^{*\prime\prime}$ a total derivative?
options: It equals $\partial_x(\psi^*\psi^\prime-\psi\psi^{*\prime})$: the cross terms $\psi^{*\prime}\psi^\prime$ cancel
whys.explain: Differentiate the bracket: $\psi^{*\prime}\psi^\prime+\psi^*\psi^{\prime\prime}-\psi^\prime\psi^{*\prime}-\psi\psi^{*\prime\prime}$.

variant.change: A complex potential $V=V_R-\frac i2\Gamma$ with a constant $\Gamma>0$ (an absorbing region).
variant.changed: The potential terms no longer cancel: each gives $-\frac{\Gamma}{2\hbar}|\psi|^2$.
variant.result: $\partial_t\rho+\partial_xj=-\frac\Gamma\hbar\rho$: probability is lost at the rate $\Gamma/\hbar$.

parts: Let $\Psi(x,t)$ be a solution of the time-dependent Schroedinger equation (one dimension). The probability density is $\rho(x,t)=|\Psi(x,t)|^2$.
(i) Show the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\partial_xj=0$, where $j$ is the probability current that you should define. [4 pt]

items.title: Spin precession in a magnetic field
items.goal: Spin $\frac12$ with $\hat H=\omega\hat S_z$ (from $\hat H=-\gamma\mathbf B\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}$ with $\mathbf B=B\hat z$, $\omega=-\gamma B$). The spin starts along $+x$. Find $\langle\hat{\mathbf S}\rangle(t)$.
lines: Eigenstates $|\!\uparrow\rangle$, $|\!\downarrow\rangle$ with energies $\pm\frac{\hbar\omega}2$.
$|\psi(0)\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt2}(|\!\uparrow\rangle+|\!\downarrow\rangle)$, so $|\psi(t)\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt2}\big(e^{-i\omega t/2}|\!\uparrow\rangle+e^{i\omega t/2}|\!\downarrow\rangle\big)$.
Up to a global phase: $\frac1{\sqrt2}\big(|\!\uparrow\rangle+e^{i\omega t}|\!\downarrow\rangle\big)$, the spin state pointing at the azimuth $\varphi=\omega t$ in the $xy$ plane.
$\langle\hat S_x\rangle=\frac\hbar2\cos\omega t$, $\langle\hat S_y\rangle=\frac\hbar2\sin\omega t$, $\langle\hat S_z\rangle=0$: the spin precesses about $\mathbf B$ with angular frequency $\omega$.
moves: Energy eigenstates of the field direction
Each component picks up $e^{-iEt/\hbar}$
Only the relative phase matters: it is the azimuth of the spin

whys.q: Why may the factor $e^{-i\omega t/2}$ be dropped?
options: A global phase does not change any expectation value
whys.explain: Only the relative phase between the components is measurable; here it grows as $\omega t$, which is the precession.

variant.change: The field points along $x$: $\hat H=\omega\hat S_x$, and the spin starts in $|\!\uparrow\rangle$.
variant.task: Find the probability to find $|\!\downarrow\rangle$ at time $t$.
variant.changed: Now $|\!\uparrow\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt2}(|+x\rangle+|-x\rangle)$ is the superposition, and the phase builds up between $|\pm x\rangle$.
variant.result: The spin rotates about $x$: $\langle\hat S_z\rangle=\frac\hbar2\cos\omega t$ and $P_\downarrow(t)=\sin^2\frac{\omega t}2$ (a full flip after $t=\pi/\omega$).

exam.label: Spin-1/2 and spin-1 in a magnetic field, time evolution

parts: D.2 [3] A spin-polarised state $|\psi\rangle=(|\uparrow\rangle-i|\downarrow\rangle)/\sqrt2$ is exposed to a magnetic field in the $z$ direction. Compute the time evolution of $\mathbf S=\langle\psi(t)|\hat{\mathbf S}|\psi(t)\rangle$.

A particle of charge $q$ and spin 1 (spin is its only degree of freedom) has $H=-\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf B=\frac qm\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$; in the $S_3$ basis $S_1=\frac\hbar{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $S_3=\hbar\,\mathrm{diag}(1,0,-1)$.

a) For a constant homogeneous field along $x_3$, compute $|\psi(t)\rangle$ for the state that at $t=0$ is the eigenstate of $S_1$ with eigenvalue $+\hbar$ (check: $(\frac12,\frac1{\sqrt2},\frac12)^T$). [3 P]

where.note: Not a named section: it combines the spin-1/2 rotation formula (7.5, script (7.60)) with the Zeeman Hamiltonian (9.6).

items.title: Fermi’s golden rule
items.goal: A constant perturbation $\hat V$ is switched on at $t=0$. Derive the transition rate from $|i\rangle$ into a continuum of final states with density $\rho(E)$.
lines: First order in the interaction picture: $c_f(t)=\frac1{i\hbar}\int_0^t\langle f|\hat V|i\rangle e^{i\omega_{fi}t^\prime}dt^\prime$ with $\omega_{fi}=(E_f-E_i)/\hbar$.
$c_f(t)=-\frac{V_{fi}}{\hbar\omega_{fi}}\big(e^{i\omega_{fi}t}-1\big)$.
$|c_f(t)|^2=\frac{|V_{fi}|^2}{\hbar^2}\,\frac{\sin^2(\omega_{fi}t/2)}{(\omega_{fi}/2)^2}$.
For large $t$, $\frac{\sin^2(\omega t/2)}{(\omega/2)^2}\to2\pi t\,\delta(\omega)$: $|c_f|^2\to\frac{2\pi}\hbar|V_{fi}|^2\,t\,\delta(E_f-E_i)$, growing linearly in $t$.
Sum over the continuum, $\sum_f\to\int dE_f\,\rho(E_f)$: the rate is $\Gamma=\frac{2\pi}\hbar|V_{fi}|^2\rho(E_i)$.
moves: First-order amplitude: integral of the matrix element with the phase
The squared amplitude is a peak in energy of width about $2\pi/t$ and height $t^2$
Its area grows like $t$; summing over the continuum gives a constant rate

whys.q: Why does a continuum of final states give a constant rate, while a single final state only oscillates?
options: Summing over states, the peak (height $\propto t^2$, width $\propto1/t$) has an area $\propto t$
whys.explain: For one final state $|c_f|^2$ oscillates and never grows without bound; only the sum over many nearly degenerate states turns into a rate.

items.title: Variational method
items.goal: Show $E_0\le\langle\psi|\hat H|\psi\rangle$ for every normalised $\psi$, and apply it to the oscillator with the trial function $\psi_b\propto e^{-bx^2}$.
lines: Expand $\psi=\sum_nc_n|n\rangle$ in eigenstates: $\langle\hat H\rangle=\sum_n|c_n|^2E_n\ge E_0\sum_n|c_n|^2=E_0$.
For $\psi_b=(2b/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-bx^2}$: $\langle x^2\rangle=\frac1{4b}$ and $\langle p^2\rangle=\hbar^2b$, so $E(b)=\frac{\hbar^2b}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^2}{8b}$.
$E^\prime(b)=0$: $\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}=\frac{m\omega^2}{8b^2}$, so $b=\frac{m\omega}{2\hbar}$.
$E(b)=\frac{\hbar\omega}4+\frac{\hbar\omega}4=\frac{\hbar\omega}2$: exact, because the true ground state is in the trial family.
